# Documents in a relational database

A `JSONB` column holds a whole JSON document, stored in a binary form that Postgres can index, next
to the ordinary typed columns of the same row. It suits data whose shape varies from row to row,
such as optional attributes or payloads kept exactly as they arrived, and SQLAlchemy exposes each
JSONB operator as a Python expression. The one behavior to keep in mind is that a missing key reads
as SQL `NULL`, which changes the result of any filter that negates a comparison.

## Reading values out

The arrow operators read a value by key. `->` returns it as JSON and `->>` as text, and a cast turns
the text into a typed value:

| SQL | SQLAlchemy | result |
|---|---|---|
| `payload -> 'k'` | `Event.payload["k"]` | jsonb |
| `payload ->> 'k'` | `Event.payload["k"].astext` | text |
| `payload #>> '{a,b}'` | `Event.payload[("a", "b")].astext` | text, nested |
| `(payload ->> 'k')::int` | `Event.payload["k"].as_integer()` | integer |

Each of them returns `NULL` when the key is missing.

## Containment queries

Most filters on JSONB use containment, `@>`, which asks whether a document includes a given
fragment. A GIN index can answer this kind of query without reading every row:

```python
select(Event).where(Event.payload.contains({"user": {"plan": "pro"}}))
```

## Negation and missing keys

A negated comparison skips every row where the key is absent. `payload ->> 'device' != 'web'`
evaluates to `NULL` for a row with no `device` key, because `NULL != 'web'` is `NULL`, and `WHERE`
keeps only rows where the condition is true. When a missing key should count as "not web", the
query has to include those rows explicitly, as in
`or_(Event.payload["device"].astext != "web", ~Event.payload.has_key("device"))`.

## Unnesting arrays

`jsonb_array_elements` turns a row that holds an array into one row per element, and from there
`WHERE`, `GROUP BY` and `JOIN` work as on any table. In SQLAlchemy, `.table_valued(...)` makes the
function usable in `FROM`, and a join `ON true` has Postgres evaluate it once for each row:

```python
item = func.jsonb_array_elements(Event.payload["items"]).table_valued(column("value", JSONB))
select(Event.id, item.c.value["sku"].astext).join(item, true())
```

`jsonb_to_recordset` does the same with typed columns instead of a single `jsonb` value, which saves
the casts when the elements share a shape.

## Paths and updates

Postgres 12 added the SQL/JSON path language for queries inside a single document, much like `jq`.
The path `$.items[*] ? (@.qty > 1)`, for example, selects the items whose quantity is above one.

Updates use operators too. `||` merges two documents, `-` removes a key, `#-` removes a path, and
`jsonb_set` writes a value at a path, while `RETURNING` sends the changed document back in the
same round trip.

::: {.callout-tip}
## JSONB or columns

Values that are filtered, joined or aggregated routinely belong in typed columns, and JSONB is for
the rest, such as per-row attributes, payloads stored as received, and settings. A GIN index with
`jsonb_path_ops` makes containment fast, but a JSONB key stays more expensive to query than a typed
column.
:::
